prompt: Let $V$ be a $10$-dimensional real vector space and $U_1$ and $U_2$ two linear subspaces such that $U_1\subseteq U_2$, $\dim_{\mathbb R}U_1=3$ and $\dim_{\mathbb R}U_2=6$. Let $\mathcal E$ be the set of all linear maps $T:V\to V$ which have $U_1$ and $U_2$ as invariant subspaces (i.e., $T(U_1)\subseteq U_1$ and $T(U_2)\subseteq U_2$). Calculate the dimension of $\mathcal E$ as a real vector space.

solutions.title: Block upper-triangular matrices
solutions.body:
Choose a basis $v_1,v_2,v_3$ of $U_1$, extend it by $v_4,v_5,v_6$ to a basis of $U_2$, and by $v_7,\dots,v_{10}$ to a basis of $V$. A linear map $T$ lies in $\mathcal E$ iff
- $Tv_1,Tv_2,Tv_3\in U_1=\operatorname{span}(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, and
- $Tv_4,Tv_5,Tv_6\in U_2=\operatorname{span}(v_1,\dots,v_6)$

(invariance only needs to be checked on a basis of each subspace; then $T(U_1)\subseteq U_1\subseteq U_2$ handles $v_1,v_2,v_3$ for $U_2$ too). So in this basis the matrix of $T$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks of sizes $3,3,4$:
$$\begin{bmatrix}*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times4}\\0&*_{3\times3}&*_{3\times4}\\0&0&*_{4\times4}\end{bmatrix},$$
and every such matrix occurs. $\mathcal E$ is the subspace of matrices with these free entries: columns $1$–$3$ have $3$ free entries each, columns $4$–$6$ have $6$ each, columns $7$–$10$ have $10$ each:
$$\dim\mathcal E=3\cdot3+3\cdot6+4\cdot10=9+18+40=67.$$
**Answer: $67$**

solutions.title: Count the forced zeros
solutions.body:
Of the $100$ entries of a $10\times10$ matrix (in the adapted basis above), the forced zeros are: in the $3$ columns of $v_1,v_2,v_3$ the $7$ rows $4$–$10$, i.e. $21$ zeros; in the $3$ columns of $v_4,v_5,v_6$ the $4$ rows $7$–$10$, i.e. $12$ zeros. All other entries are free, so $\dim\mathcal E=100-21-12=67$.

**Answer: $67$**

prompt:
Prove that the following proposition holds for $n=3$ (5 points) and $n=5$ (7 points), and does not hold for $n=4$ (8 points).

"For any permutation $\pi_1$ of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ different from the identity there is a permutation $\pi_2$ such that any permutation $\pi$ can be obtained from $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ using only compositions (for example, $\pi=\pi_1\circ\pi_1\circ\pi_2\circ\pi_1$)."
answer: The proposition says $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle=S_n$. $n=3$: pair a transposition with a 3-cycle (Lagrange). $n=4$: fails for $\pi_1=(12)(34)$, since $S_4/V_4$ has order $6$ but no element of $S_4$ has order divisible by $6$. $n=5$: explicit partners for one representative of each of the $6$ cycle types, e.g. $(12)$ & $(12345)$, $(123)$ & $(12)(345)$, $(12)(34)$ & $(135)(24)$, $(1234)$ & $(45)$, $(123)(45)$ & $(34)$.

solutions.title: Reduce to generation, then check each cycle type
solutions.body:
**Reformulation.** In a finite group every element has finite order, so $g^{-1}=g^{k-1}$ where $k$ is the order of $g$. Hence the set of all compositions of $\pi_1,\pi_2$ is the subgroup $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle$, and the proposition says: for every $\pi_1\ne\mathrm{id}$ there is $\pi_2$ with $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle=S_n$.

It suffices to check one permutation of each cycle type: if $\pi_1=\sigma x\sigma^{-1}$ and $\langle x,y\rangle=S_n$, then $\langle\pi_1,\sigma y\sigma^{-1}\rangle=\sigma\langle x,y\rangle\sigma^{-1}=S_n$. We use the rule $\sigma(a\,b)\sigma^{-1}=(\sigma(a)\,\sigma(b))$ and the fact that the transpositions $(1\,k)$, $k=2,\dots,n$, generate $S_n$ (every permutation is a product of transpositions and $(a\,b)=(1\,a)(1\,b)(1\,a)$).

**$n=3$.** If $\pi_1$ is a transposition, take $\pi_2=(1\,2\,3)$; if $\pi_1$ is a $3$-cycle, take $\pi_2=(1\,2)$. In both cases $\langle\pi_1,\pi_2\rangle$ contains elements of orders $2$ and $3$, so by Lagrange its order is divisible by $6=|S_3|$.

**$n=4$ fails.** Let $x=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ and $V=\{\mathrm{id},(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$, a normal subgroup of $S_4$ with $|S_4/V|=6$. Suppose $\langle x,y\rangle=S_4$. Since $x\in V$, the quotient $S_4/V$ is generated by $yV$, so $yV$ has order $6$. But the order of $yV$ divides the order of $y$, and elements of $S_4$ have orders $1,2,3,4$ — none divisible by $6$. Contradiction; so no $\pi_2$ exists for $\pi_1=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.

**$n=5$.** The non-identity cycle types are $(12)$, $(123)$, $(12)(34)$, $(1234)$, $(123)(45)$, $(12345)$.
1. $x=(1\,2)$, $y=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$: conjugating $x$ by $y,y^2,y^3$ gives $(2\,3),(3\,4),(4\,5)$; the adjacent transpositions generate $S_5$. Symmetrically, for $x=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ take $y=(1\,2)$.
2. $x=(1\,2\,3)$, $y=(1\,2)(3\,4\,5)$: $y^3=(1\,2)$ and $y^4=(3\,4\,5)$. Conjugating $(1\,2)$ by $x$ and $x^2$ gives $(2\,3),(3\,1)$. Conjugating $(1\,3)$ by $(3\,4\,5)$ and its square gives $(1\,4),(1\,5)$. So all $(1\,k)$ lie in the subgroup: it is $S_5$.
3. $x=(1\,2)(3\,4)$, $y=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$: $y^3=(2\,4)$, $y^4=(1\,3\,5)$. Then $x(2\,4)x^{-1}=(1\,3)$; $(1\,3\,5)$ conjugates $(1\,3)$ to $(3\,5)$; $x$ conjugates $(3\,5)$ to $(4\,5)$. The transpositions $(1\,3),(3\,5),(5\,4),(4\,2)$ form a path through all five points, and they generate $S_5$ (e.g. $(1\,5)=(1\,3)(3\,5)(1\,3)$, and so on along the path).
4. $x=(1\,2\,3\,4)$, $y=(4\,5)$: conjugating $(4\,5)$ by $x,x^2,x^3$ gives $(1\,5),(2\,5),(3\,5)$; the transpositions $(k\,5)$ generate $S_5$.
5. $x=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5)$, $y=(3\,4)$: $x^3=(4\,5)$, $x^4=(1\,2\,3)$. Conjugating $(3\,4)$ by $(1\,2\,3)$ and its square gives $(1\,4),(2\,4)$; together with $(3\,4),(4\,5)$ we have all $(k\,4)$, which generate $S_5$.

So the proposition holds for $n=3$ and $n=5$ and fails for $n=4$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f(x)=2x(1-x)$, $x\in\mathbb R$. Define $f_n=\underbrace{f\circ\dots\circ f}_{n}$.

a) Find $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}\displaystyle\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$.

b) Compute $\displaystyle\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx$ for $n=1,2,\dots$.

solutions.title: Closed form for the iterates
solutions.body:
**b)** Note $f(x)=\frac12-2\left(x-\frac12\right)^2$. We claim
$$f_n(x)=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\left(x-\tfrac12\right)^{2^n}\qquad(n\ge1).$$
For $n=1$ this is the identity above. If it holds for $n$, then
$$f_{n+1}(x)=f_n(f(x))=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\Bigl(-2\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^2\Bigr)^{2^n}=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\,2^{2^n}\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^{2^{n+1}}=\frac12-2^{2^{n+1}-1}\bigl(x-\tfrac12\bigr)^{2^{n+1}}.$$
Integrating,
$$\int_0^1f_n(x)\,dx=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\left[\frac{(x-\frac12)^{2^n+1}}{2^n+1}\right]_0^1=\frac12-2^{2^n-1}\cdot\frac{2\cdot2^{-(2^n+1)}}{2^n+1}=\frac12-\frac1{2(2^n+1)}.$$
(Check: $n=1$ gives $\frac13=\int_0^12x(1-x)\,dx$.)

**a)** Letting $n\to\infty$: $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1f_n=\frac12$.

**Answer: a) $\frac12$; b) $\frac12-\frac1{2(2^n+1)}$.**

solutions.title: Monotone convergence for part a)
solutions.body:
Fix $x_0\in(0,1)$ and let $x_n=f_n(x_0)$. Then $x_1=2x_0(1-x_0)\in(0,\frac12]$, and for $t\in(0,\frac12]$ we have $f(t)-t=t(1-2t)\ge0$ and $f(t)\le\frac12$. So $(x_n)_{n\ge1}$ is nondecreasing and bounded by $\frac12$; its limit $l>0$ satisfies $l=2l(1-l)$, i.e. $l=\frac12$. Thus $f_n\to\frac12$ pointwise on $(0,1)$, with $0\le f_n\le\frac12$ on $[0,1]$, and by dominated convergence $\int_0^1f_n\to\frac12$.

**Answer to a): $\frac12$.**

prompt:
The function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable and satisfies $f(0)=2$, $f'(0)=-2$ and $f(1)=1$. Prove that there exists a real number $\xi\in(0,1)$ for which
$$f(\xi)\cdot f'(\xi)+f''(\xi)=0.$$
answer: $g=\frac12f^2+f'$ has $g'=ff'+f''$ and $g(0)=0$; find $\eta\in(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$ (Rolle for $h=\frac x2-\frac1f$ if $f$ has no zero, otherwise IVT between the first and last zero of $f$), then apply Rolle to $g$ on $[0,\eta]$.

solutions.title: An auxiliary function $g=\frac12f^2+f'$
solutions.body:
Let $g(x)=\frac12f(x)^2+f'(x)$. It is differentiable with $g'=ff'+f''$, and $g(0)=\frac12\cdot4-2=0$. So it suffices to find $\eta\in(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$: Rolle's theorem on $[0,\eta]$ then gives $\xi\in(0,\eta)\subset(0,1)$ with $g'(\xi)=0$.

**Case 1: $f$ has no zero in $[0,1]$.** Then $h(x)=\frac x2-\frac1{f(x)}$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$ and $h(0)=-\frac12=\frac12-1=h(1)$. By Rolle there is $\eta\in(0,1)$ with
$$0=h'(\eta)=\frac12+\frac{f'(\eta)}{f(\eta)^2}=\frac{g(\eta)}{f(\eta)^2},$$
so $g(\eta)=0$.

**Case 2: $f$ has a zero in $[0,1]$.** The zero set is closed and, as $f(0)=2$, $f(1)=1$, contained in $(0,1)$. Let $z_1$ and $z_2$ be the smallest and largest zeros. Since $f>0$ on $[0,z_1)$,
$$f'(z_1)=\lim_{x\to z_1^-}\frac{f(x)-0}{x-z_1}\le0,$$
and since $f>0$ on $(z_2,1]$, $f'(z_2)=\lim_{x\to z_2^+}\frac{f(x)}{x-z_2}\ge0$. So $g(z_1)=f'(z_1)\le0\le f'(z_2)=g(z_2)$. As $g$ is continuous ($f'$ is differentiable), the intermediate value theorem gives $\eta\in[z_1,z_2]\subset(0,1)$ with $g(\eta)=0$.

In both cases we are done. ∎

*Remark.* $f(x)=\frac2{x+1}$ satisfies the hypotheses and $ff'+f''\equiv0$.

prompt:
Let $P$ be an algebraic polynomial of degree $n$ having only real zeros and real coefficients.

a) Prove that for every real $x$ the following inequality holds:
$$(n-1)\bigl(P'(x)\bigr)^2\ge nP(x)P''(x).\tag{2}$$

b) Examine the cases of equality.
answer: With $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$: $(n-1)\frac{P'^2}{P^2}-n\frac{P''}{P}=\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2\ge0$. For $n\ge2$, equality at $x$ holds iff $x$ is a multiple zero of $P$ or all zeros of $P$ coincide ($P=c(x-a)^n$, equality for every $x$); for $n=1$ both sides vanish identically.

solutions.title: Logarithmic derivative
solutions.body:
If $n=1$ then $P''\equiv0$ and both sides of (2) are $0$, so equality always holds. Let $n\ge2$ and $P(x)=c\prod_{i=1}^n(x-x_i)$ with real $x_i$ (with multiplicity) and $c\ne0$.

**At a zero $x=x_i$:** the right side is $0$ and the left side is $(n-1)P'(x_i)^2\ge0$, with equality iff $P'(x_i)=0$, i.e. iff $x_i$ is a multiple zero.

**At $x$ with $P(x)\ne0$:** put $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$. Then
$$\frac{P'}{P}=\sum_ia_i,\qquad \frac{P''}{P}=\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)'+\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2=-\sum_ia_i^2+\Bigl(\sum_ia_i\Bigr)^2=2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j.$$
Hence
$$(n-1)\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-n\frac{P''}{P}=(n-1)\sum_ia_i^2+2(n-1)\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j-2n\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j=(n-1)\sum_ia_i^2-2\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j=\sum_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2\ge0.$$
Multiplying by $P(x)^2>0$ gives (2).

**b) Equality** at such an $x$ holds iff all $a_i$ are equal, i.e. $x_1=\dots=x_n$. So, for $n\ge2$: equality holds at $x$ iff $x$ is a multiple zero of $P$, or all zeros of $P$ coincide. In the latter case $P=c(x-a)^n$, and indeed $(n-1)n^2c^2(x-a)^{2n-2}=n\cdot c(x-a)^n\cdot n(n-1)c(x-a)^{n-2}$ for all $x$: (2) is an identity exactly for these polynomials. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
For $P(x)\ne0$ and $a_i=\frac1{x-x_i}$ as above, $\frac{P'}{P}=\sum a_i$ and $\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-\frac{P''}{P}=-\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)'=\sum a_i^2$. By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\bigl(\sum a_i\bigr)^2\le n\sum a_i^2$, i.e.
$$\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2\le n\Bigl(\Bigl(\frac{P'}{P}\Bigr)^2-\frac{P''}{P}\Bigr)\iff nP P''\le(n-1)P'^2,$$
with equality iff all $a_i$ are equal, i.e. all zeros coincide. At zeros of $P$ argue as in the first solution. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function with the property that for any $x$ and $y$ in the interval,
$$xf(y)+yf(x)\le1.$$
a) Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\le\frac\pi4$.

b) Find a function, satisfying the condition, for which there is equality.
answer: a) Substituting $x=\sin\theta$ and $x=\cos\theta$: $2\int_0^1f=\int_0^{\pi/2}\bigl(\cos\theta f(\sin\theta)+\sin\theta f(\cos\theta)\bigr)d\theta\le\frac\pi2$. b) $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.

solutions.title: Two trigonometric substitutions
solutions.body:
**a)** Let $I=\int_0^1f(x)\,dx$. The substitutions $x=\sin\theta$ and $x=\cos\theta$ ($\theta\in[0,\frac\pi2]$) give
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(\sin\theta)\cos\theta\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}f(\cos\theta)\sin\theta\,d\theta.$$
Adding and applying the hypothesis with $x=\sin\theta$, $y=\cos\theta$ (both in $[0,1]$):
$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\bigl(\sin\theta\,f(\cos\theta)+\cos\theta\,f(\sin\theta)\bigr)d\theta\le\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,d\theta=\frac\pi2 .$$
So $I\le\frac\pi4$.

**b)** Let $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$, continuous on $[0,1]$. For $x,y\in[0,1]$ write $x=\sin\theta$, $y=\sin\varphi$ with $\theta,\varphi\in[0,\frac\pi2]$; then $f(x)=\cos\theta$, $f(y)=\cos\varphi$ and
$$xf(y)+yf(x)=\sin\theta\cos\varphi+\cos\theta\sin\varphi=\sin(\theta+\varphi)\le1 .$$
Its integral is the area of a quarter of the unit disc, $\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx=\frac\pi4$, so equality holds. ∎

prompt: Let $V$ be a real vector space, and let $f,f_1,f_2,\dots,f_k$ be linear maps from $V$ to $\mathbb R$. Suppose that $f(x)=0$ whenever $f_1(x)=f_2(x)=\dots=f_k(x)=0$. Prove that $f$ is a linear combination of $f_1,f_2,\dots,f_k$.
answer: $\Phi=(f_1,\dots,f_k):V\to\mathbb R^k$ has $\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$, so $f=L\circ\Phi$ for a linear $L$ on $\Phi(V)$; extend $L$ to $\mathbb R^k$, $L(t)=\sum c_it_i$, giving $f=\sum c_if_i$.

solutions.title: Factor through $\mathbb R^k$
solutions.body:
Let $\Phi:V\to\mathbb R^k$, $\Phi(x)=(f_1(x),\dots,f_k(x))$, a linear map. The hypothesis says $\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$.

Define $L:\Phi(V)\to\mathbb R$ by $L(\Phi(x))=f(x)$. This is well defined: if $\Phi(x)=\Phi(x')$ then $x-x'\in\ker\Phi\subseteq\ker f$, so $f(x)=f(x')$. It is linear because $f$ and $\Phi$ are. The image $W=\Phi(V)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb R^k$; extend a basis of $W$ to a basis of $\mathbb R^k$ and define $L$ to be $0$ on the added vectors. This gives a linear functional on $\mathbb R^k$, which has the form $L(t_1,\dots,t_k)=c_1t_1+\dots+c_kt_k$. Hence for all $x\in V$
$$f(x)=L(\Phi(x))=c_1f_1(x)+\dots+c_kf_k(x).\ \blacksquare$$

solutions.title: Induction with a dual system of vectors
solutions.body:
Induction on $k$; the case $k=0$ (then $f\equiv0$) is trivial. Discarding some $f_i$ that are linear combinations of the others does not change the common kernel, so we may assume $f_1,\dots,f_k$ are linearly independent.

For each $j$ there is $a_j\in V$ with $f_i(a_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$ and $f_j(a_j)=1$: otherwise $f_j$ vanishes on $\bigcap_{i\ne j}\ker f_i$, and by the induction hypothesis (with $k-1$ functionals) $f_j$ would be a combination of the others, contradicting independence; then normalize. Now for any $x\in V$ the vector $z=x-\sum_jf_j(x)a_j$ satisfies $f_i(z)=f_i(x)-f_i(x)=0$ for all $i$, so $f(z)=0$, i.e.
$$f(x)=\sum_{j=1}^kf(a_j)\,f_j(x).\ \blacksquare$$

prompt:
Let
$$\mathcal P=\Bigl\{f:\ f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^3a_kx^k,\ a_k\in\mathbb R,\ |f(\pm1)|\le1,\ \bigl|f(\pm\tfrac12)\bigr|\le1\Bigr\}.$$
Evaluate
$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal P}\ \max_{-1\le x\le1}|f''(x)|$$
and find all polynomials $f\in\mathcal P$ for which the above "sup" is attained.
answer: The supremum is $24$, attained exactly for $f=\pm T_3=\pm(4x^3-3x)$. Key formula: $f''(1)=\frac{16}3f(1)-\frac{28}3f(\tfrac12)+\frac{20}3f(-\tfrac12)-\frac83f(-1)$ (and symmetrically for $f''(-1)$).

solutions.title: Express $f''(\pm1)$ through the four values
solutions.body:
Write $A=f(-1)$, $B=f(-\frac12)$, $C=f(\frac12)$, $D=f(1)$ for $f=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+a_3x^3$. Then
$$D+A=2a_0+2a_2,\quad C+B=2a_0+\tfrac12a_2\ \Rightarrow\ a_2=\tfrac23(A+D-B-C),$$
$$D-A=2a_1+2a_3,\quad C-B=a_1+\tfrac14a_3\ \Rightarrow\ a_3=\tfrac23\bigl(D-A-2C+2B\bigr).$$
Since $f''(x)=6a_3x+2a_2$ is linear, $\max_{[-1,1]}|f''|=\max(|f''(1)|,|f''(-1)|)$, and
$$f''(1)=6a_3+2a_2=\tfrac{16}3D-\tfrac{28}3C+\tfrac{20}3B-\tfrac83A,$$
$$f''(-1)=-6a_3+2a_2=\tfrac{16}3A-\tfrac{28}3B+\tfrac{20}3C-\tfrac83D.$$
For $f\in\mathcal P$, $|A|,|B|,|C|,|D|\le1$, so by the triangle inequality
$$|f''(\pm1)|\le\tfrac{16+28+20+8}3=24 .$$
**Equality.** $|f''(1)|=24$ forces $|A|=|B|=|C|=|D|=1$ with the signs of $D,C,B,A$ equal to $\varepsilon\cdot(+,-,+,-)$ for a common $\varepsilon=\pm1$, i.e. $(A,B,C,D)=\varepsilon(-1,1,-1,1)$. A cubic is determined by its values at four points (Lagrange interpolation), and the Chebyshev polynomial $T_3(x)=4x^3-3x$ takes the values $T_3(-1)=-1$, $T_3(-\frac12)=1$, $T_3(\frac12)=-1$, $T_3(1)=1$. Hence $f=\varepsilon T_3$. Likewise $|f''(-1)|=24$ forces $(A,B,C,D)=\varepsilon(1,-1,1,-1)$, i.e. again $f=\pm T_3$.

Conversely $\pm T_3\in\mathcal P$ and $|T_3''(x)|=|24x|$ has maximum $24$ on $[-1,1]$.

**Answer: the supremum is $24$, attained exactly for $f(x)=\pm(4x^3-3x)$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $0<c<1$ and
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac xc,&x\in[0,c],\\[2mm]\dfrac{1-x}{1-c},&x\in[c,1].\end{cases}$$
We say that $p$ is an $n$-periodic point if
$$\underbrace{f(f(\dots f}_{n}(p)))=p$$
and $n$ is the smallest number with this property. Prove that for every $n\ge1$ the set of $n$-periodic points is non-empty and finite.
answer: $f^n$ consists of $2^n$ affine pieces, each mapping its interval onto $[0,1]$, so $f^n$ has exactly $2^n$ fixed points. At most $2+4+\dots+2^{n-1}=2^n-2$ of them have a smaller period, so at least $2$ (and finitely many) are $n$-periodic.

solutions.title: Count fixed points of the iterates
solutions.body:
Let $f^n$ denote the $n$-th iterate.

**Claim.** $[0,1]$ is the union of $2^n$ closed intervals $J$ with disjoint interiors such that on each $J$ the map $f^n$ is affine and maps $J$ bijectively onto $[0,1]$.

For $n=1$ take $[0,c]$ and $[c,1]$. If the claim holds for $n$, take a piece $J$ for $f^n$; since $f^n|_J$ is an affine bijection onto $[0,1]$, the preimages of $[0,c]$ and $[c,1]$ split $J$ into two closed subintervals, and on each of them $f^{n+1}=f\circ f^n$ is a composition of affine bijections onto $[0,1]$. This gives $2^{n+1}$ pieces.

**Fixed points of $f^n$.** Let $J=[s,t]$ be a piece. Its length is $<1$ (there are $2^n\ge2$ pieces), so $f^n|_J$ has slope $\pm\frac1{t-s}$ with absolute value $>1$; therefore $f^n(x)-x$ is strictly monotone on $J$. If $f^n$ increases on $J$, then $f^n(s)-s=-s\le0$ and $f^n(t)-t=1-t\ge0$; if it decreases, $f^n(s)-s=1-s\ge0$ and $f^n(t)-t=-t\le0$. Either way $f^n$ has exactly one fixed point in $J$. A fixed point cannot be a common endpoint of two pieces: such an endpoint $e$ lies in $(0,1)$ while $f^n(e)\in\{0,1\}$. Hence $f^n$ has exactly $2^n$ fixed points.

**Conclusion.** Every $n$-periodic point is a fixed point of $f^n$, so there are finitely many. A fixed point of $f^n$ that is not $n$-periodic is a fixed point of some $f^k$ with $1\le k\le n-1$; there are at most $2+2^2+\dots+2^{n-1}=2^n-2$ such points. So at least $2^n-(2^n-2)=2$ fixed points of $f^n$ are $n$-periodic; in particular the set is non-empty. ∎

prompt:
Let $A_n=\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, where $n\ge3$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of all non-constant functions $f:A_n\to A_n$ satisfying the following conditions:

(1) $f(k)\le f(k+1)$ for $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$,

(2) $f(k)=f(f(k+1))$ for $k=1,2,\dots,n-1$.

Find the number of functions in $\mathcal F$.
answer: $\binom n3$. Every $f\in\mathcal F$ is $f(i)=k$ for $i\le m$, $f(m+1)=l$, $f(i)=i-1$ for $i\ge m+2$, with $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$; these correspond to the $3$-subsets $\{k<l<m+1\}$ of $A_n$.

solutions.title: Structure of the functions
solutions.body:
**The functions.** For $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$ define
$$f_{k,l,m}(i)=\begin{cases}k,&i\le m,\\ l,&i=m+1,\\ i-1,&i\ge m+2.\end{cases}$$
It is nondecreasing ($k<l$, and $l\le m<m+1=f(m+2)$) and non-constant. Condition (2): for $i\le m-1$, $f(f(i+1))=f(k)=k$ since $k\le m$; for $i=m$, $f(f(m+1))=f(l)=k=f(m)$ since $l\le m$; for $i=m+1$, $f(f(m+2))=f(m+1)$; for $i\ge m+2$, $f(f(i+1))=f(i)$. So $f_{k,l,m}\in\mathcal F$.

**Every $f\in\mathcal F$ is of this form.** Let $f\in\mathcal F$ and $k=f(1)$.
1. *A value taken twice is a fixed point.* If $f(i)=f(i+1)=v$ then by (2) $f(v)=f(f(i+1))=f(i)=v$. Such a pair exists: otherwise $f$ is strictly increasing, hence the identity, but the identity violates (2) ($k\ne k+1$).
2. *If $f(v)=v$ then $f\equiv v$ on $\{1,\dots,v\}$.* Indeed if $f(j)=v$ for some $j\ge2$, then $f(j-1)=f(f(j))=f(v)=v$; descend from $j=v$. In particular $v=f(1)=k$: **$k$ is the only fixed point**, $f\equiv k$ on $\{1,\dots,k\}$, and by 1 (a value taken twice by a nondecreasing function is taken at two consecutive places) every value other than $k$ is taken at most once.
3. Let $m=\max\{i:f(i)=k\}$. Then $k\le m\le n-1$ ($f$ is non-constant), $f\equiv k$ on $\{1,\dots,m\}$ by monotonicity, and $f$ is strictly increasing on $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$ with values $>k$.
4. *$f(i)<i$ for $i>m$.* $f(i)=i$ is impossible ($i>k$ would be a second fixed point). If $f(i)>i$ for some $i>m$, strict increase gives $f(n)\ge f(i)+(n-i)>n$, impossible.
5. *$f(i)=i-1$ for $i\ge m+2$.* Here $f(i)>f(m+1)>k$. If $f(i)\le m$ then $f(i-1)=f(f(i))=k$, contradicting $i-1\ge m+1$. So $m+1\le f(i)\le i-1$, and $f(f(i))=f(i-1)$ with both $f(i)$ and $i-1$ in $\{m+1,\dots,n\}$, where $f$ is injective; hence $f(i)=i-1$.
6. Put $l=f(m+1)$; by 3 and 4, $k<l\le m$.

So $f=f_{k,l,m}$, and different triples give different functions.

**Counting.** $(k,l,m)\mapsto\{k,l,m+1\}$ is a bijection from triples with $1\le k<l\le m\le n-1$ onto the $3$-element subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (since $k<l<m+1\le n$). Hence
$$|\mathcal F|=\binom n3 .$$
(For example $n=3$: only $f=(1,1,2)$; $n=4$: four functions.) ∎

prompt: Suppose that $\mathcal S$ is a family of spheres (i.e., surfaces of balls of positive radius) in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, such that the intersection of any two contains at most one point. Prove that the set $M$ of those points that belong to at least two different spheres from $\mathcal S$ is countable.
answer: Each $x\in M$ is a tangency point of two spheres $S,T$ of $\mathcal S$. Code $x$ by a label (external/internal tangency) and two rational points: in $B(S),B(T)$ for external tangency, in the shell $B(S)\setminus\overline{B(T)}$ and in $B(T)$ for internal tangency ($T$ inside $S$). Since open balls of spheres in $\mathcal S$ are disjoint or nested, the code determines $x$.

solutions.title: Encode each point by rational points in balls
solutions.body:
For a sphere $S$ with centre $a$ and radius $r$ let $B(S)$ be the open ball and $\overline B(S)$ the closed ball.

**Fact.** Let $S\ne S'$ be spheres (centres $a,a'$, radii $r,r'$, $d=|a-a'|$) meeting in at most one point. Then either $d\ge r+r'$ — the open balls are disjoint and the closed balls meet in at most one point — or $d\le|r-r'|$ — the balls are nested, e.g. $B(S')\subseteq B(S)$ if $r'\le r$. Indeed, if $|r-r'|<d<r+r'$, a triangle with sides $d,r,r'$ exists, and rotating it about the line $aa'$ (possible as $n\ge2$) produces at least two common points. In particular, **any two open balls of (equal or distinct) spheres of $\mathcal S$ are disjoint or nested.**

For each $x\in M$ fix spheres $S\ne T$ in $\mathcal S$ through $x$; then $S\cap T=\{x\}$, so by the Fact either
- (E) $B(S)\cap B(T)=\varnothing$ and $\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)=\{x\}$ (external tangency), or
- (I) after renaming, $B(T)\subsetneq B(S)$ and $S\cap T=\{x\}$ (internal tangency).

Choose points with rational coordinates: in case (E), $u\in B(S)$, $v\in B(T)$; in case (I), $u\in B(S)\setminus\overline B(T)$ (a nonempty open shell) and $v\in B(T)$. Map $x\mapsto(\text{label},u,v)$, a map into the countable set $\{E,I\}\times\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q^n$. We show it is injective; then $M$ is countable.

**Two points of type (E) with the same code.** Let $x,x'$ come from $(S,T)$ and $(S',T')$ with $u\in B(S)\cap B(S')$, $v\in B(T)\cap B(T')$. These pairs of balls intersect, so they are nested; by symmetry assume $B(S)\subseteq B(S')$.
- If $B(T)\subseteq B(T')$: $\{x\}=\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)\subseteq\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T')=\{x'\}$, so $x=x'$.
- If $B(T')\subseteq B(T)$: compare $B(S')$ and $B(T)$. $B(S')\subseteq B(T)$ is impossible ($u\in B(S)\subseteq B(S')$ but $B(S)\cap B(T)=\varnothing$), and so is $B(T)\subseteq B(S')$ ($v\in B(T')\subseteq B(T)$ but $B(S')\cap B(T')=\varnothing$); in particular $S'\ne T$. So $B(S')\cap B(T)=\varnothing$ and $\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T)$ has at most one point. Both $x\in\overline B(S)\cap\overline B(T)$ and $x'\in\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T')$ lie in $\overline B(S')\cap\overline B(T)$; hence $x=x'$.

**Two points of type (I) with the same code.** Now $u\in(B(S)\setminus\overline B(T))\cap(B(S')\setminus\overline B(T'))$, $v\in B(T)\cap B(T')$. By symmetry $B(T)\subseteq B(T')$. The balls $B(T')$ and $B(S)$ both contain $v$, so they are nested; $B(S)\subseteq B(T')$ is impossible since $u\in B(S)$, $u\notin\overline B(T')$. Hence $B(T')\subsetneq B(S)$. Now $x\in\overline B(T)\subseteq\overline B(T')$ and $x\in S$, so $x\notin B(T')\subseteq B(S)$; thus $x\in T'$. The balls $B(S),B(S')$ share $u$, so they are nested:
- If $B(S)\subseteq B(S')$: $x'\in T'\subseteq\overline B(T')\subseteq\overline B(S)$ and $x'\in S'$, so $x'\notin B(S)$; hence $x'\in S$. So $x,x'\in T'\cap S$ with $T'\ne S$, and $x=x'$.
- If $B(S')\subseteq B(S)$: $x\in\overline B(T')\subseteq\overline B(S')$ and $x\in S$, so $x\notin B(S')$, i.e. $x\in S'$. So $x,x'\in T'\cap S'$ with $T'\ne S'$, and $x=x'$.

Hence the coding is injective and $M$ is countable. ∎

prompt:
Let $f:(0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ be a function that is zero except at the distinct points $a_1,a_2,\dots$. Let $b_n=f(a_n)$.

(a) Prove that if $\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n<\infty$, then $f$ is differentiable at at least one point $x\in(0,1)$.

(b) Prove that for any sequence of non-negative real numbers $(b_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ with $\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n=\infty$, there exists a sequence $(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ such that the function $f$ defined as above is nowhere differentiable.
answer: (a) Choose $c_n\to\infty$ with $\sum c_nb_n<\frac12$; the intervals $(a_n-c_nb_n,a_n+c_nb_n)$ have total length $<1$, and at any uncovered $x_0$ the difference quotients are $\le1/c_n$, so $f'(x_0)=0$. (b) Choose $\beta_n\le b_n$, $\beta_n\to0$, with block sums $\ge1$; place the $a_n$ so that each block's intervals of length $\beta_n$ cover $(0,1)$; then every $x_0$ has $a_n$ within $\beta_n$ with quotient $\ge1$.

solutions.title: Small covering intervals
solutions.body:
**Preliminary.** If $f$ is differentiable at $x_0$, then $f(x_0)=0$ and $f'(x_0)=0$. Indeed $f$ vanishes outside a countable set, so every interval contains points where $f=0$. If $f(x_0)>0$, then $f$ is not continuous at $x_0$. If $f(x_0)=0$, the difference quotient is $0$ along points $x\to x_0$ with $f(x)=0$, so $f'(x_0)=0$.

**(a)** If all $b_n=0$, $f\equiv0$. Otherwise let $B=\sum b_n>0$. Since the tails $\sum_{n\ge N}b_n\to0$, choose $N_1<N_2<\dots$ with $\sum_{n\ge N_k}b_n\le4^{-k}$, and put $c_n=1$ for $n<N_1$ and $c_n=2^k$ for $N_k\le n<N_{k+1}$. Then $c_n\to\infty$ and
$$\sum_nc_nb_n\le B+\sum_{k\ge1}2^k\sum_{n\ge N_k}b_n\le B+\sum_k2^{-k}=B+1 .$$
Replacing $c_n$ by $c_n/(4(B+1))$ we get $c_n\to\infty$ and $\sum c_nb_n\le\frac14$.

Let $I_n=(a_n-c_nb_n,\,a_n+c_nb_n)$ (empty if $b_n=0$). Their total length is $\le\frac12<1$, so they do not cover $(0,1)$: otherwise, for small $\delta>0$ the compact set $[\delta,1-\delta]$ would be covered by finitely many $I_n$, forcing $1-2\delta\le\frac12$. Take $x_0\in(0,1)$ in no $I_n$. Then $f(x_0)=0$ (if $x_0=a_n$, then $b_n=0$). For $x\ne x_0$: if $f(x)=0$ the difference quotient is $0$; if $x=a_n$ with $b_n>0$, then $|a_n-x_0|\ge c_nb_n$, so
$$\left|\frac{f(a_n)-f(x_0)}{a_n-x_0}\right|\le\frac{b_n}{c_nb_n}=\frac1{c_n}.$$
Given $\varepsilon>0$, only finitely many $n$ have $1/c_n\ge\varepsilon$, and the corresponding $a_n$ are at positive distance from $x_0$. So in a small neighbourhood of $x_0$ all difference quotients are $<\varepsilon$: $f'(x_0)=0$.

**(b)** Since $\sum b_n=\infty$, also $\sum\min(b_n,1)=\infty$, hence $\sum_{n\ge s}\min(b_n,\frac1k)\ge\frac1k\sum_{n\ge s}\min(b_n,1)=\infty$ for every $s,k$. So we can split $\mathbb N$ into consecutive finite blocks $J_1,J_2,\dots$ with $\sum_{n\in J_k}\beta_n\ge1$, where $\beta_n=\min(b_n,\frac1k)$ for $n\in J_k$. Thus $0\le\beta_n\le b_n$ and $\beta_n\le\frac1k$ on $J_k$.

Choose the $a_n$ block by block. In block $J_k$, list the $n$ with $\beta_n>0$ in order and lay consecutive closed intervals $[L_n,R_n]$ of length $\beta_n$ starting at $0$ ($L=0$, $R=\beta_n$, the next one starts where the previous ends), stopping once some $R_n\ge1$; as the lengths sum to $\ge1$, these intervals cover $[0,1]$. For each such $n$ pick $a_n\in(L_n,R_n)\cap(0,1)$ different from all previously chosen points (possible: a nonempty open interval is infinite). For all remaining $n$ pick any new point $a_n\in(0,1)$. The $a_n$ are distinct.

Let $x_0\in(0,1)$. If $f(x_0)>0$, $f$ is not differentiable at $x_0$ by the preliminary remark. If $f(x_0)=0$: for each $k$ some $n\in J_k$ has $x_0\in[L_n,R_n]$, so $|a_n-x_0|\le\beta_n\le\frac1k$, and $a_n\ne x_0$ because $f(a_n)=b_n\ge\beta_n>0$. Then
$$\frac{|f(a_n)-f(x_0)|}{|a_n-x_0|}\ge\frac{b_n}{\beta_n}\ge1 .$$
So there are points arbitrarily close to $x_0$ with difference quotient $\ge1$, contradicting $f'(x_0)=0$. Hence $f$ is nowhere differentiable. ∎
